facts.statement: Fossils of Zatomus have been found in North Carolina, United States.
facts.quote: Fossil remains have been found in North Carolina, United States.

facts.statement: American geologist Ebenezer Emmons discovered and described the fossils of Zatomus in North Carolina.
facts.quote: The fossils of Zatomus were discovered in North Carolina by American geologist Ebenezer Emmons, who described and illustrated the fossils.

facts.statement: The fossils of Zatomus consist of teeth and dermal plates.
facts.quote: These fossils consisted of teeth and dermal plates.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope named the species Zatomus sarcophagus in 1871 based on fossil teeth that he thought resembled those of Megalosaurus, Laelaps, or Teratosaurus.
facts.quote: Edward Drinker Cope thought the fossil teeth resembled those of a dinosaur similar to Megalosaurus, Laelaps, or the rauisuchian Teratosaurus, and in 1871 he named Zatomus sarcophagus, based on the teeth.

facts.statement: Zatomus belongs to the unranked order Crurotarsi.
Zatomus belongs to the order Rauisuchia.
Zatomus was classified within the ancient order Thecodontia, a group of archosaurs that were ancestors of dinosaurs.
facts.quote: Estaba clasificado dentro del antiguo orden de los Thecodontia, un tipo de arcosaurios que eran los antepasados de los dinosaurios.

facts.statement: Zatomus lived during the Late Triassic, between 225 and 208 million years ago.
facts.quote: que vivió a finales del triásico, entre 225-208 millones de años

facts.statement: The parent group of Zatomus is Teratosauridae.
Zatomus is classified in the family Teratosauridae.
The Paleobiology Database lists the time range for Zatomus as the Campanian, from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Campanian to Campanian (83.6 to 72.2 million years ago)

rejected.statement: Zatomus is classified as a rauisuchian, a type of large carnivorous thecodontian archosaur.
rejected.quote: It is classified as a rauisuchian, a type of large carnivorous thecodontian archosaur.
